They say that good things come to those who wait. That's oftentimes true in the NFL, even though the bulk of offseason additions are made during early free agency and in the draft.

The reality is that, while the top veterans are usually off the board after the initial wave of free agency, many quality players will wait for the right opportunity to reveal itself just before or during training camp. Other meaningful late additions are often made as legitimate playoff contenders look to fill needs after fully evaluating their rosters.

These trends have continued in 2026, and several notable players joined teams during the late summer. Some of them could even help spark Super Bowl runs—or, at least, provide realistic hopes of playing for a championship.

Here, we'll examine the notable summer additions most likely to influence the Super Bowl picture based on factors like past performance, positional value, projected roles, and team construction.

The Houston Texans reached the divisional round of last year's playoffs thanks to a defense that ranked first overall and second in points allowed. If they can pair that level of defensive dominance with an improved offense, they could go a step or two further in the postseason.

A lot will hinge on the play of quarterback C.J. Stroud, who has regressed since being the 2023 Offensive Rookie of the Year. Having a better supporting cast around Stroud, however, will certainly help his cause.

The Texans added running back David Montgomery and revamped their offensive line yet again by adding the likes of Evan Brown, Wyatt Teller, and Keylan Rutledge . In August, they added wide receiver Kayshon Boutte in a trade with the New England Patriots.

Boutte is coming off a 556-yard, six-touchdown campaign with New England and could play a critical role in the Texans' offense this season. Houston lacked dependable targets behind Nico Collins in 2025, and it recently lost No. 2 receiver Jayden Higgins to a torn ACL.

Higgins caught 41 passes for 525 yards and six touchdowns with Houston last season.

Should Boutte provide a reliable perimeter target opposite Collins and help Houston's offense approach top-10 status, the Texans should be one of the toughest outs in the AFC playoff field.

Boutte wasn't the only notable late addition that Houston made this offseason.

The Texans certainly weren't short on defensive playmakers entering August, but they added another one when they brought back former franchise standout Jadeveon Clowney.

The first overall pick in the 2014 draft, Clowney spent his first five seasons in Houston before being traded to the Seattle Seahawks in 2019. After spending the past several seasons as a journeyman pass-rusher, he is back where it all began.

"I've grown up and learned the game a lot more since leaving," Clowney said, per Jonathan M. Alexander of the Houston Chronicle . "I feel like I can help the younger guys. I've learned how to lead and what it takes to get to a Super Bowl. I feel like I can help this team."

Clowney is a luxury addition for the Texans' defense, but he can legitimately influence the team's chances of reaching Super Bowl LXI. After joining the Dallas Cowboys as a late 2025 addition, he tallied 8.5 sacks, 12 tackles for loss, and 22 quarterback pressures.

As a third option behind Danielle Hunter and Will Anderson Jr., Clowney can help give the Texans the most relentless edge-rushing rotation in the league. That could be enough to carry Houston deep into the playoffs, even if its offense only shows minor improvements.

The Washington Commanders aren't widely viewed as Super Bowl contenders entering Week 1. The team battled injuries and an atrocious defense in 2025 while stumbling to a 5-12 record.

Of course, Washington wasn't viewed as a contender in 2024, either, but Daniels led the team to the NFC title game as a rookie.

Having Daniels healthy might not be enough to put Washington back in the playoff picture, but defensive additions like K'Lavon Chaisson, Rasul Douglas, Nick Cross, and Odafe Oweh should help. So will wide receiver Stefon Diggs, who was signed in August to complement No. 1 receiver Terry McLaurin.

During Daniels' Offensive Rookie of the Year campaign, tight end Zach Ertz was the only truly reliable target Washington had behind McLaurin.

Diggs is coming off a 1,000-yard season and a trip to the Super Bowl, and he's now another year removed from his 2024 ACL tear.

The 32-year-old believes Washington couldn't have landed a better second option.

"You can't name a No. 2 better than me," Diggs said on his YouTube channel (h/t ESPN ).

Daniels and the Commanders will have to recapture their 2024 magic to make any meaningful postseason run this season. If Diggs can help bolster the passing attack, though, Washington's Super Bowl hopes will also see a boost.

B/R NFL Scouting Dept's 2027 NFL Mock Draft Before 2026 Season

As the defending Super Bowl champs, the Seattle Seahawks don't have many glaring roster needs. However, they do have some question marks in the secondary after losing Riq Woolen and Coby Bryant in free agency.

Seattle added cornerback Trevon Diggs in August. While he didn't make the 53-man roster, he was added to the practice squad with the expectation that he'll contribute in 2026.

"He's just getting ramped up as you saw the other night just getting his legs under him. But he's confident and we're excited to get him going and see how far he can take this thing," general manager John Schneider said, per Ari Horton of the team's official website.

Before suffering a torn ACL in 2023, Diggs was a Dallas Cowboys Pro Bowler and one of the biggest turnover threats in the league. He hasn't played particularly well since the injury, but he showed glimpses of his previous form by snagging an interception during Seattle's preseason.

The Seahawks' hopes of returning to the Super Bowl won't hinge on Diggs' contributions. However, Seattle has to feel confident about having a potential difference-maker waiting in the wings at one of the game's most important positions.

While the other players on this list joined new teams late in the summer, three-time Defensive Player of the Year Aaron Donald returned from a two-year retirement to rejoin the only NFL franchise he has known, the Los Angeles Rams.

The Rams were already widely considered the preseason Super Bowl favorites before Donald's comeback became official. L.A. reached last year's NFC title game, employs the reigning MVP in quarterback Matthew Stafford, and added the reigning Defensive Player of the Year by trading for Myles Garrett.

Adding Donald to the mix could give Los Angeles one of the league's most formidable defensive fronts, though the Rams will likely manage his return cautiously.

"Looks like himself, but you know he's 35 years old; they want to make sure they ramp him up the right way," ESPN's Jeremy Fowler said on SportsCenter (h/t Bleacher Report's Scott Polacek ).

The Rams should have had high Super Bowl hopes before adding Donald to the roster. After adding him, anything short of a Super Bowl berth will probably be viewed as a disappointment.

The Cowboys haven't reached the NFC title game since they won it all following the 1995 season. However, Dallas has real reasons to believe it can make a Super Bowl run in 2026.

A year ago, the Cowboys possessed one of the league's most explosive offenses, though it was wasted by a historically bad defense. However, the core of that offense remains intact, while Dallas has invested heavily in its defense.

Dating back to last year's trade deadline, the Cowboys have added the likes of Quinnen Williams, Jalen Thompson, Rashan Gary, Cobie Durant, Caleb Downs , and Malachi Lawrence . On August 16, they also added future Hall of Famer Von Miller.

As an eight-time Pro Bowler, two-time champion and one-time Super Bowl MVP, Miller brings a wealth of experience and leadership to Dallas' defense. He can also still play at a high level.

Last season with the Commanders, Miller recorded nine sacks, six tackles for loss, and 19 quarterback pressures. In Dallas, he might be the proverbial final piece of the defensive puzzle, which should at least allow the Cowboys to dream about a Super Bowl return.

If Dallas can pair the sort of offense it had last year with a defense that is even average, it can make some real noise in the postseason.

Harrison Smith is the most recent addition to this list, having re-signed with the Minnesota Vikings on Saturday. After contemplating his future for virtually the entire offseason, the safety is back for a 15th NFL season.

Smith had previously been released with a post-June 1 designation, but both he and Minnesota were open to another run.

Like the Commanders, the Vikings are coming off a disappointing season and aren't widely viewed as legitimate contenders. However, it's important to remember Minnesota won nine games last year and 14 games in 2024. The difference in those two records largely came down to quarterback play.

With Sam Darnold providing a steady presence behind center two years ago, the Vikings had a shot at the NFC's No. 1 seed until the final week. With J.J. McCarthy and other signal-callers providing inconsistent QB play, the Vikings were a non-factor in the playoffs—but still good enough to yield a winning record.

With Kyler Murray set to pursue his redemption arc in Minnesota, the Vikings could be closer to what they were in 2024 than what we saw in 2025.

Bringing back Smith will do nothing to help the offense, but it will help ensure that Minnesota has a capable defense. The 37-year-old appeared in 15 games last season and tallied 54 tackles, a sack, two interceptions, and a forced fumble.

In other words, the Vikings now have a more complete roster than they had just a few days ago.

articles.title: B/R Experts Week 1 NFL Power Rankings
articles.summary: After months of pre-draft predictions, free-agency frenzy, draft-day surprises, OTAs, minicamps, training camp and the preseason, it's time to play NFL games that count.
articles.body:
After months of pre-draft predictions, free-agency frenzy, draft-day surprises, OTAs, minicamps, training camp and the preseason, it's time to play NFL games that count.

With all that excitement comes a mountain of uncertainty. The NFL has a habit of reminding people that what they think they know and what they actually know are two different things.

Predictions of a Seahawks-Patriots Super Bowl at this time last year were rare.

Every Sunday is a wild ride, and the landscape is constantly changing.

Still, you have to start somewhere. Square 1 is where you'll find Bleacher Report NFL analysts Gary Davenport , Kris Knox , Maurice Moton and Brent Sobleski ranking all 32 teams from worst to first entering the regular season.

Miami Dolphins fans could be in for a difficult 2026 season.

By just about any estimation, the Dolphins have the weakest roster in the league after purging veterans all offseason.

The team signed Malik Willis to start under center after he showed some promise in Green Bay, but he's made all of six starts in four seasons. Miami has an electric young running back in De'Von Achane, but that's it where offensive weapons are concerned.

Defensively, Jordyn Brooks and rookie Jacob Rodriguez are a solid duo at linebacker, and Zach Sieler is a quality tackle. But there are major questions on the edge and on the back end, and in today's pass-heavy NFL that's a dangerous combination.

The Dolphins are in Stage 1 of a ground-up rebuild, and it's going to show this season. — Davenport

The Arizona Cardinals are entering an evaluation season.

If anything, the slight chance of outperforming expectations should be viewed as a negative since Arizona won't surpass the other three teams in the NFC West and could hurt its draft standing, which is vitally important to ensure the acquisition of a top quarterback prospect.

Some will look at this setup as a defeatist attitude. They wouldn't be wrong, either.

At the same time, the Cardinals can't consistently compete based on how their roster is currently constructed.

New head coach Mike LaFleur gets a mulligan campaign until he can help with the selection process of the team's next quarterback. — Sobleski

Our experts all seem to agree that the Cleveland Browns are a bottom-tier team, and that probably says more about their quarterback situation than anything else.

The Browns have some talented young players on their roster and the bones of a defense that ranked fourth overall last season—with Jared Verse trying to replace the departed Myles Garrett.

Even with Garrett leading the defense, though, Cleveland couldn't notch more than five wins, in large part because of bad quarterback play.

The return of Deshaun Watson doesn't really improve the Browns' QB situation, and the looming 2027 quarterback class could eventually leave Cleveland searching for fewer wins than it got a year ago. — Knox

B/R NFL Scouting Dept's 2027 NFL Mock Draft Before 2026 Season

Late NFL Additions Who Could Influence 2026 Super Bowl Hopes

The Jets are a franchise stuck in limbo—and it's partly of their own doing.

On one hand, the team hopes to be building a foundation for the future. New York had three first-round picks in 2026 and is set to have three more in a 2027 draft that is projected to be loaded at quarterback.

However, the Jets have also been reluctant to fully embrace a rebuild. The addition of veteran quarterback Geno Smith is unlikely to get them into the playoffs or deliver their first winning season since 2015.

The Jets have enough talent on both sides of the ball to win 5-6 games with competent quarterback play—and all that will do is make it that much harder to draft an elite quarterback prospect in 2027 without moving up. — Davenport

Atlanta enters the 2026 season with significant questions on both sides of the ball.

In terms of offensive weapons, the Falcons are set up well. Running back Bijan Robinson, wide receiver Drake London and tight end Kyle Pitts are an impressive trio, and the offensive line is solid.

However, Atlanta headed into Week 1 without having named a starting quarterback, and that's not a good sign.

Defensively, things are even worse. We already knew the linebacker position was going to be a potential concern, but a Falcons team that led the NFC in sacks last season will now be down its top two edge-rushers for at least the first eight games—and one is out for the season.

Those absences create a major problem for the defense.

The NFC South is widely viewed as one of the league's weakest divisions, but Atlanta's issues entering the season may be too much to overcome. — Davenport

The Tennessee Titans are slowly building toward something of substance and should be far more competitive this fall.

The pieces are falling into place after the back-to-back top-10 selections of quarterback Cam Ward and wide receiver Carnell Tate.

The organization signed Wan'Dale Robinson as a free agent to give Ward another quality target.

Defensively, Tennessee experienced an overhaul under the watchful eye of new head coach Robert Saleh. The additions of John Franklin-Myers, Jordan Elliott, Jermaine Johnson II, Jacob Martin, Solomon Thomas, Cor'Dale Flott, Alontae Taylor and Joshua Williams, as well as first- and second-round rookies Keldric Faulk and Anthony Hill Jr., provide a significant boost on that side of the ball.

Ward needs to show growth in Year 2. Tennessee's offensive line must hold together. And the defense should jell over time. As these things progress, the Titans will be viewed as a difficult matchup. — Sobleski

Coming off a 3-14 campaign, the Las Vegas Raiders should be able to build early momentum in their home opener against the Miami Dolphins, who are also in the early phases of a rebuild.

Kirk Cousins played in new head coach Klint Kubiak's system during his time with the Minnesota Vikings in 2021. He should be solid behind a revamped offensive line that features three-time Pro Bowl center Tyler Linderbaum.

While the Raiders' offense will be much improved, their secondary will be inexperienced and susceptible to big plays. First-time defensive coordinator Rob Leonard is a question mark. His ability to put the young defensive backs in spots to succeed could make or break the defense. — Moton

Everyone is eager to see Jayden Daniels return to the form he showcased as Offensive Rookie of the Year two seasons ago.

However, I'm not convinced that having the quarterback healthy and playing at a high level will be enough to return Washington to contention.

This is a team that had serious flaws in 2025 that extended beyond its injury issues. Its offense was short on playmakers, and its defense was the worst in the league in terms of yards allowed.

The Commanders will have to prove they're better, not just healthier, on both sides of the ball to rise in our power rankings. — Knox

The New York Giants should be instantly more competitive with John Harbaugh taking over as head coach. He knows what it takes to build a contender and to sustain success, and fans should expect to see glimpses of that in 2026.

However, we're probably still a year away from seeing New York make a real run in the NFC East. Despite having several promising young players, the Giants still have a lot of unknowns.

Much will hinge on Jaxson Dart's ability to stay healthy and make a significant second-year jump. — Knox

The Indianapolis Colts are running it back this year, though significant lingering concerns exist. Injuries will play the biggest factor.

Quarterback Daniel Jones may be cleared and ready to start in Week 1, but he's still coming off a torn Achilles tendon. Wide receiver Alec Pierce finally practiced fully last week after ankle surgery, but he missed all of training camp and the preseason. Tight end Tyler Warren is dealing with a groin injury. Top rookie CJ Allen dealt with injuries throughout his first training camp, which means he's not fully ready for the regular season.

Meanwhile, the defensive trio of DeForest Buckner, Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward are coming off injuries last season that should be considered worrisome.

The talent found on Indianapolis' roster is obvious, but the squad's depth is thin. If the Colts are going to play like the team that showed up during the first half of last season, its top players must remain on the field. – Sobleski

It's now or never for Bryce Young and the Carolina Panthers.

Winning a division at 8-9 was hardly dominant, but a title is a title, and the Panthers showed promise at times last season—most notably with a Week 13 win over the Rams.

The Panthers exercised Young's 2027 option, though Yahoo Sports reported that his future as Carolina's starter could be in doubt if he does not take a significant step forward in his fourth season. He surpassed 3,000 passing yards last season but has yet to throw for 25 touchdowns in a single year.

There are weapons in Carolina in wideouts Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker. The Panthers spent big adding free agents on defense in linebacker Devin Lloyd and edge-rusher Jaelan Phillips.

But it's still a flawed team—led by a flawed quarterback. — Davenport

Expect head coach Kevin O'Connell to open up the playbook with the most talented quarterback he's had in his tenure with the Minnesota Vikings.

Kyler Murray has played through one full season in five years, but he's still a dynamic quarterback when healthy. In Minnesota, he shouldn't have to use his legs much with Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, Jauan Jennings and T.J. Hockenson downfield.

Murray is a strong Comeback Player of the Year candidate, and he'll play with a top-notch defense led by Brian Flores that will take some pressure off the offense. Don't be surprised if the Vikings are in contention for a division title this year. — Moton

For years, some fans and analysts have called on the New Orleans Saints to begin a full rebuild after five consecutive seasons without a playoff appearance.

To date, general manager Mickey Loomis has resisted that approach, and the decision is reflected in the 2026 roster.

To be fair, if Tyler Shough can build on a promising rookie season under center, the offense could make some noise—wide receiver Chris Olave is coming off his best season, and Travis Etienne Jr. should add some pop in the backfield. The defense was quietly ninth in the league in total defense in 2025.

The Saints could win a weak NFC South this season, but they are not a Super Bowl contender—and it is difficult to see a path to becoming one while they remain committed to chasing the fringes of playoff contention. — Davenport

The Pittsburgh Steelers feel like the wild card of the AFC North.

They have enough overall talent to make some postseason noise if the reunion between Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers is successful. However, an aging roster and some notable holes could also leave Pittsburgh out of the playoff mix early if Rodgers regresses.

This is a team that ranked 25th and 26th in yards gained and yards allowed, respectively, last season. We should learn quickly whether former coach Mike Tomlin was holding the Steelers back or holding them together. — Knox

Prior to last year, the Buccaneers had won four straight NFC South titles. But a 6-2 start in 2025 turned into a 2-7 finish, followed by a missed postseason and a rocky offseason.

Todd Bowles enters 2026 under significant pressure, while Baker Mayfield faces unresolved contract uncertainty. Franchise stalwarts such as wide receiver Mike Evans and Lavonte David are gone.

Reinforcements have arrived, but they aren't Evans and David.

The Buccaneers are the betting favorites in the NFC South, but there are real questions with just about every position group on this roster.

Tampa could win the division, or wind up in the basement. — Davenport

The Kansas City Chiefs are in the middle of the power-ranking pack because they need to convince us they're closer to the team that was a Super Bowl contender before their 6-11 campaign in 2025. Although Patrick Mahomes is on track to suit up for Week 1, there are still questions about the roster.

As the No. 1 receiver, can Rashee Rice stay healthy? Is Xavier Worthy going to make a third-year leap? How effective will Travis Kelce be in his 14th year? Can Jaylon Moore be a reliable right tackle? How will the secondary hold up following an offseason of changes?

There are just too many questions, aside from how Mahomes bounces back from a torn ACL, to think the Chiefs belong back in the top half of our power rankings. — Moton

Quarterback Jordan Love must carry the Green Bay Packers through the first several weeks of the season.

Running back Josh Jacobs is on the commissioner's exempt list. The team placed edge-rusher Micah Parsons on the physically unable to perform list, which means he'll miss at least four games.

Green Bay's cornerback group is shaky, with Keisean Nixon and Carrington Valentine on the boundary. Both allowed passer ratings above 105 and gave up 13 touchdowns combined in coverage last year.

In 2024 and 2025, the Packers ranked in the bottom six in pass attempts. Love has the playmakers to lead a productive passing attack, but he'll have to compensate for a potentially leaky defense and unproven running backs in the ground game. Green Bay could stumble to the NFC North basement early if he can't. — Moton

It may be now or never for the Cincinnati Bengals.

After years of seemingly only investing in offensive players who could help sell tickets, Cincinnati put some work into rebuilding its defense. If new pieces like Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, and Cashius Howell can help the Bengals be just average defensively, they should be a playoff team.

That is, of course, assuming that Joe Burrow can stay healthy, which isn't guaranteed. If he does and Cincinnati misses the playoffs again anyway, fans can probably expect a regime change. — Knox

The Dallas Cowboys had one of the NFL's most potent offenses last season. Unfortunately, they also had a historically bad defense that was the first in franchise history to surrender more than 500 points in a season.

The good news is that the bulk of last year's offense remains intact, while the Cowboys added several promising pieces to their defense in the offseason. Even moderate improvements on defense should be enough to make Dallas a legitimate playoff threat. — Knox

The Chicago Bears should make more strides in their second season under head coach Ben Johnson. In all four of his years as an offensive play-caller, he's fielded a top-nine scoring offense, three as a coordinator with the Detroit Lions and last season.

Any one of Luther Burden III, Rome Odunze or Colston Loveland could break out this year while D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai share touches in an effective ground attack.

Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen must cover holes on his side of the ball, though. Safety Coby Bryant will be out for a few months after undergoing knee surgery. The team traded defensive tackle Gervon Dexter Sr. to the Atlanta Falcons, which leaves Pro Bowler Montez Sweat as the only reliable pass-rusher on the front line.

The Bears are still a playoff-caliber squad, but their defensive question marks could be an issue against tough opponents. — Moton

Although the Detroit Lions will open the season without safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, they're explosive enough on offense to reach their Week 6 bye with a winning record.

The Lions' home opener against the New Orleans Saints could be a tight battle, but Detroit will face the New York Jets, Carolina Panthers and Arizona Cardinals before its bye, three teams that aren't high-scoring juggernauts.

If Joseph and Branch are back in October, the Lions' momentum should take off during a stretch in which the team plays one road game between Weeks 7 and 12.

New offensive coordinator Drew Petzing can help get the offense on track during a favorable home stretch as the secondary gets healthy. There's a lot to like about the Lions, both in their roster and schedule. — Moton

Our experts seem to agree that the Baltimore Ravens will be back in the playoff picture this season. They might even be title contenders if they can fix a few key issues from the 2025 season.

Baltimore was a missed kick away from winning the AFC North last season, but it never quite felt like a team that could challenge the AFC's best. If Jesse Minter can dramatically improve last year's 24th-ranked defense and Lamar Jackson can stay healthy, the Ravens can be the sort of conference threat they were just two years ago. — Knox

The Los Angeles Chargers are usually offseason darlings, though they have earned it under head coach Jim Harbaugh, going 11-6 in back-to-back seasons. The Chargers have also deservedly garnered criticism for their lack of playoff success.

As the panelist who ranked the Chargers slightly outside the top 10 (No. 13), it's fair to note the loss of former defensive coordinator Jesse Minter, who took over as head coach of the Baltimore Ravens.

Sure, this team will score a lot of points under new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, but it may also struggle to keep defenses out of the end zone as the players adjust to first-year play-caller Chris O'Leary. — Moton

The Philadelphia Eagles are the team to beat in the NFC East, and they might even be a little underrated heading into Week 1.

Dallas' defensive overhaul and John Harbaugh's arrival in New York soaked up much of the divisional spotlight during the offseason. However, Philly has made four playoff appearances, won three division titles, appeared in two Super Bowls, and lifted one Lombardi Trophy over the past four seasons.

With A.J. Brown gone, the inexperienced Sean Mannion taking over as offensive coordinator and some shuffling in the secondary, the Eagles could regress. If those unknowns prove to be non-issues, though, they could also make their way back to the title game. — Knox

Kyle Shanahan's squad has been hit hard by injuries over the years. At the same time, the Niners remain one of the league's most competitive teams.

In five of the last seven seasons, San Francisco has made the postseason. Shanahan and Co. own a 72-45 record during that stretch.

There's no reason to expect this year's team to take a step back this fall, not with Fred Warner, Nick Bosa and George Kittle back in the lineup despite coming off season-ending injuries.

From there, the Niners front office reworked the wide receiver room by signing Mike Evans, drafting De'Zhaun Stribling and re-signing Deebo Samuel. Also, the acquisition of Osa Odighizuwa should provide an interior pass-rush presence to help the squad's edge-defenders and hopefully create far more pressure than last season.

On paper, the 49ers are set. Everyone needs to stay on the field, though. — Sobleski

The Jacksonville Jaguars were already the NFL's best team over the second half of the 2025 regular season. Granted, Liam Coen's squad lost in the first round of the postseason. Even so, this year's squad can be even more dangerous.

Obviously, quarterback Trevor Lawrence finally lived up to his potential, with the chance to build off that performance. Travis Hunter is back and healthy after playing in only seven games as a rookie. Also, the Jaguars will now have a full season with wide receiver Jakobi Meyers in the lineup.

Despite last season's ending, the Jags should be excited about what they can do this fall. But the team needs a full season of consistent performance, not just half of one. — Sobleski

The Patriots experienced a seismic turnaround in Mike Vrabel's first season as head coach, going from a four-win team in 2024 to a 13-win AFC champion in 2025.

The question now is if they can back that success up.

Offensively, the team should be formidable. Quarterback Drake Maye looks the part of a superstar. The arrival of A.J. Brown gives Maye a true alpha receiver. Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson offer an impressive thunder-and-lightning combination in the backfield.

However, there are potential issues. The offensive line was mauled in Super Bowl LX. The defense heads into the season without its most proven pass-rusher. After facing a historically easy schedule a year ago, the Patriots open this season against four consecutive 2025 playoff teams, including road games at Seattle, Jacksonville and Buffalo.

New England could lose as many games in September as it did all of last year. — Davenport

There isn't a team east of Los Angeles more in Super Bowl-or-bust mode than the Buffalo Bills.

The Bills dismissed their highly successful coach because he couldn't get the team over the hump. They are led by Josh Allen, who has more playoff wins than any quarterback in NFL history without a Super Bowl appearance.

The good news is the team should be in the thick of it in the AFC. The offense has the league's reigning rushing king and a new No. 1 wide receiver in D.J. Moore. The defense ranked seventh in the league last year.

The bad news is that the Bills have been in the thick of it for the better part of a decade, but for whatever reason they come up short in the postseason. — Davenport

The Houston Texans will go as far as quarterback C.J. Stroud takes them. He doesn't need to operate at any MVP standard for the Texans to become a serious Super Bowl contender, either.

Houston's defense is already good enough to place the team among the NFL's best. The quarterback simply needs to be better than what's been seen the last two seasons and closer to how he performed as a rookie.

The pieces are now around him after the acquisition of running back David Montgomery and the front office reworking the offensive line.

For most NFL teams, the idea of playing complementary football is getting enough from a defense to ensure the squad's high-flying offense doesn't find itself in a shootout every week. In Houston's case, its defense dictates terms.

However, the Texans need to consistently move the ball offensively. If Stroud and Co. do so, the AFC will be ripe for the taking. — Sobleski

The Denver Broncos head into the 2026 season fully loaded.

With the exception of edge-rusher Jonathon Cooper, who's on the commissioner's exempt list, they return most of their third-ranked scoring defense from the previous year.

Bo Nix made a full recovery from two ankle surgeries, and he'll have a new lead receiver in Jaylen Waddle. Going into his third year with an established big-play wideout, Nix can elevate the passing attack to a top-10 unit under head coach Sean Payton.

Most of our panelists agree that Denver is a top-three team to open the season, which seems fitting for a club coming off an AFC Championship appearance. — Moton

Typically, the reigning Super Bowl champions receive the benefit of the doubt heading into the following campaign. The Seattle Seahawks are still considered one of the NFC's best teams. However, the current makeup of the squad could realistically make them the NFC West's third-best team depending on how things break this fall.

First, the Seahawks must adjust offensively without Klint Kubiak calling plays and the reigning Super Bowl MVP, Kenneth Walker III, serving as the lead back. Defensively, the trio of Riq Woolen, Boye Mafe and Coby Bryant departed in free agency.

Seattle remains a veteran and experienced group, which should prevent any post-Super Bowl slump. At the same time, slight regression shouldn't be unexpected based on where the team currently stands. — Sobleski

Anything short of a Super Bowl victory will be viewed as a disappointment for the Los Angeles Rams.

The addition of Myles Garrett, who is the NFL's reigning Defensive Player of the Year, and Aaron Donald coming out of retirement only made last season's NFC Championship Game participant even more dangerous.

While those two headline the franchise's offseason moves, the additions of Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson at cornerback shouldn't be overlooked, especially when the Rams finished among the bottom half of the league in pass defense in 2025.

Los Angeles now has the connective tissue between its defensive front seven and back end to thrive in all phases of the game.

As long as Matthew Stafford and the offense continues to perform at expected levels, it's hard to imagine the Rams not being the league's best team this fall. – Sobleski

articles.title: B/R NFL Scouting Dept's 2027 NFL Mock Draft Before 2026 Season
articles.summary: The 2026 college football season is officially underway, with the latest NFL campaign set to begin this coming weekend.
articles.body:
The 2026 college football season is officially underway, with the latest NFL campaign set to begin this coming weekend.

The hype for the 2027 draft cycle is already at an all-time high. Thus, the current timing serves as the perfect juncture to assess where things stand as both seasons get underway.

The Bleacher Report Scouting Department of Brandon Thorn , Dame Parson , Dan Harms and Matt Holder reconvened to project where they believe certain talent should land based on what's been seen to date.

Unsurprisingly, quarterbacks dominate the Top 10, but a wide receiver prospect veering toward legitimate "generational" status comes off the board with the No. 1 overall pick.

[Editor's Note: Draft order determined by FanDuel's reverse Super Bowl odds , with the slotting adjusted to represent NFL playoff formatting.]

1. Miami Dolphins: WR Jeremiah Smith, Ohio State

Team Fit : The Miami Dolphins are the NFL's least talented squad, hence why they're projected to own next year's No. 1 overall draft pick. Obviously, a quarterback should be in play, but Malik Willis did sign a two-year deal. Instead, Miami selects the class' No. 1 overall prospect, Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith, to give Willis a legitimate weapon.

Scout's Take : Smith blends together an elite combination of size (6'4", 222 lbs), speed, strength and ball skills. He can align anywhere to defeat either zone or man coverages. He physically dominates and can elevate an offense's efficiency.

Prospects Considered : QB Darian Mensah, Miami; QB Arch Manning, Texas; QB Dante Moore, Oregon

2. Arizona Cardinals: QB Darian Mensah, Miami

Team Fit : The Arizona Cardinals are moving forward this fall with veteran quarterback Jacoby Brissett at the helm once again. He's not the answer, and everyone understands the situation. Coincidentally, Darian Mensah follows in the footsteps of Cardinals rookie Carson Beck by taking over the Miami Hurricanes offense, though the program's latest quarterback could end up closer to Cam Ward as his class' QB1.

Scout's Take : Mensah plays with immense poise and calmness in the pocket and during big games. His ability to raise his level of play despite lacking premium talent at both Tulane and Duke displays his level of impact. Mensah plays with sound and clean mechanics, as well as the keen ability to layer passes down the field to his receiver in stride thanks to excellent ball placement.

Prospects Considered : QB Arch Manning, Texas; QB Dante Moore, Oregon; CB Leonard Moore, Notre Dame

3. New York Jets: QB Arch Manning, Texas

Team Fit : The New York Jets have three first-round draft picks in 2027. If they're not in a position to draft a quarterback, the organization has the ammunition to go get one. In this case, Arch Manning strides into the New York City market ready to complete an improving roster.

Scout's Take : Manning possesses the physical ability and flashes of processing acumen that translate to the NFL. He's still learning to become a more efficient field general, but he wins with plus-athleticism as a scrambler. Of course, Manning has the pedigree and natural ability to be a franchise cornerstone.

Prospects Considered : QB Dante Moore, Oregon; CB Leonard Moore, Notre Dame; Edge Colin Simmons, Texas

Late NFL Additions Who Could Influence 2026 Super Bowl Hopes

4. Cleveland Browns: QB Dante Moore, Oregon

Team Fit : The Cleveland Browns' decision to make Deshaun Watson their long-term quarterback has not produced the results the franchise hoped for. Granted, Shedeur Sanders must prove himself as well. In the end, the Browns are likely looking for another quarterback next April, with Oregon's Dante Moore arguably the best fit for the franchise's needs.

Scout's Take : Moore is a clean processor and smooth operator from a sound pocket. He is a stabilizing presence as a passer and when working on the move. The East Cleveland native navigates the pocket to find throwing lanes efficiently and brings a C.J. Stroud-esque level of pure natural throwing ability.

Prospects Considered : CB Leonard Moore, Notre Dame; Edge Colin Simmons, Texas; QB C.J. Carr, Notre Dame

5. Tennessee Titans: OT Trevor Goosby, Texas

Team Fit : The Tennessee Titans are taking the necessary steps to systematically build a strong talent core. With quarterback Cam Ward and wide receiver Carnell Tate already in the fold, someone to serve as the 2025 No. 1 overall pick's bodyguard is the next necessary step. Texas' Trevor Goosby can immediately upgrade Tennessee's left tackle spot.

Scout's Take : Goosby is a high-floor prospect due to a sturdy build, good length and heavy hands that are already at a level rarely seen from a player his age (21). His athletic ability is closer to average. Considering how young, big and strong he already is, his foundation signals a Year 1 NFL starter, who will be able to control the point of attack as a pro.

Prospects Considered : Edge Colin Simmons, Texas; CB Leonard Moore, Notre Dame; Edge Dylan Stewart, South Carolina

6. Las Vegas Raiders: Edge Colin Simmons, Texas

Team Fit : The Las Vegas Raiders were this close to trading Maxx Crosby this offseason. With or without Crosby next year, the lineup could still use another pass-rush threat to improve the entire defensive front. Texas' Colin Simmons is super-productive and difficult to handle working off the edge.

Scout's Take : Simmons has special movement skills to work the edges. His hand-usage remains a work-in-progress to generate clean wins more frequently, and he could afford to add some mass to become a better run-defender. Regardless, his quickness and athleticism are special. Also, the 20-year-old has a good motor to be a productive NFL sack artist.

Prospects Considered : CB Leonard Moore, Notre Dame; DL Will Echoles, Ole Miss; WR Cam Coleman, Texas

7. Carolina Panthers: CB Leonard Moore, Notre Dame

Team Fit : Mike Jackson is entering the final year of his contract. Plus, the veteran defensive back turns 30 next year. The Carolina Panthers can add an elite talent in Notre Dame's Leonard Moore, while giving Jaycee Horn a long-term bookend at outside corner.

Scout's Take : The 2027 draft class' No. 1 cornerback prospect brings a great blend of size (6'2", 215 lbs), physicality and technique to any defensive back room. Moore can play comfortably in man or zone coverage. While he isn't the class' best athlete, he's the best technician and makes up for any perceived deficiencies with a high football IQ.

Prospects Considered : Edge Dylan Stewart, South Carolina; OT Jordan Seaton, LSU; WR Cam Coleman, Texas

8. Atlanta Falcons: QB CJ Carr, Notre Dame

Team Fit : Concern continues to grow in Atlanta as the Falcons try to find out whether Tua Tagovailoa or Michael Penix Jr. can be their long-term answer at quarterback. Clearly, neither proved themselves in this scenario. The position's top tier of prospects has already been chosen, but Notre Dame's CJ Carr has a skill set that should serve him well as part of Kevin Stefanski's offensive scheme.

Scout's Take : Carr is a timing and rhythm-based passer with mobility to hurt the defense when the situation arises. He thrives operating from inside the pocket and distributing the football to his receivers. Furthermore, Carr isn't afraid to give his guys a chance to make a play.

9. New Orleans Saints: Edge Dylan Stewart, South Carolina

Team Fit : Cam Jordan is 37 years old, and the eight-time Pro Bowler expects this season to be his last. Carl Granderson's salary-cap charge also escalates to nearly $21 million next season. Chase Young's salary-cap charge tops $26 million. Some changes will be necessary, thus an opportunity to land a top-shelf edge prospect such as Dylan Stewart would be an optimal outcome.

Scout's Take : Stewart dealt with a back injury last season, which led to some regression after an impressive true freshman campaign. Still, he's an elite athlete who has enormous potential as an NFL pass-rusher, with the speed around the edge and quickness to beat offensive tackles in multiple manners. Stewart just needs to improve his hand-usage and show a better plan when his first move doesn't work.

Prospects Considered : DL Will Echoles, Ole Miss; CB Ashton Hampton, Clemson; S Brauntae Johnson, Notre Dame

10. Washington Commanders: WR Cam Coleman, Texas

Team Fit : The Washington Commanders haven't done enough to build around quarterback Jayden Daniels, specifically among the skill positions. The additions of running back Rachaad White, tight end Chig Okonkwo and wide receivers Stefon Diggs and rookie Antonio Williams will help, but none of them are legitimate difference-makers. Texas' Cam Coleman immediately gives Daniels a big-time target, particularly with Terry McLaurin getting older.

Scout's Take : Coleman possesses the physical frame and athleticism to be an NFL offense's WR1. He has great play-strength at the catch-point when extending for a pass or running short-to-intermediate routes. He has all of the traits a team wants in a potential star wideout.

Prospects Considered : WR Nick Marsh, Indiana; DL Will Echoles, Ole Miss; CB Ashton Hampton, Clemson

11. New York Giants: CB Ashton Hampton, Clemson

Team Fit : Change is likely coming to the New York Giants' cornerback room after this season. Greg Newsome II and Deonte Banks are on the last years of their current deals. Paulson Adebo has one more year remaining, though his salary-cap charge remains over $20 million in 2027. A partial reset feels necessary, and Clemson's Ashton Hampton offers high-end talent and pedigree.

Scout's Take : Hampton has all of the requisite tools to be a No. 1 corner at the NFL level. Plus, he's an explosive downhill thumper in the run game. His length and ball-tracking show up at the catch-point, while his coverage versatility makes him tough to face on a down-by-down basis.

Prospects Considered : S Brauntae Johnson, Notre Dame; DL Will Echoles, Ole Miss; OT Jordan Seaton, LSU

12. Pittsburgh Steelers: S Brauntae Johnson, Notre Dame

Team Fit : Quarterback has to be at the forefront of what the Pittsburgh Steelers do next offseason unless the organization decides to move forward with Drew Allar after a year of development. Until that decision is made (and a prospect proves worthy of this slotting), the Steelers do what they so often do: Add another talented defender. Notre Dame's Brauntae Johnson is the class' top safety to replace Jaquan Brisker, who signed a one-year deal this offseason.

Scout's Take : Physicality and size (6'2", 200 lbs) in the run game, paired with instinctual play on the back end, make Johnson a true impact playmaker. Even as the class' No. 1 safety, the junior prospect still has even room for improvement this fall.

Prospects Considered : CB Zabien Brown, Alabama; DL Will Echoles, Ole Miss; OL Trevor Lauck, Iowa

13. New York Jets (via Indianapolis): DL Will Echoles, Ole Miss

Team Fit : After landing Arch Manning earlier without having to trade up, everything from that point forward is icing on the cake for the New York Jets. The fact that Gang Green adds the class' top-graded interior defender thanks to last year's Sauce Gardner trade makes this an exceptional draft class, with another pick to go. Echoles is a highly disruptive defender capable of resetting the line of scrimmage.

Scout's Take : There's a lot to like about Echoles as a run defender. He's strong to win at the point of attack, quick off the ball to get penetration or shoot a gap and he has the lateral movement skills to avoid getting reached. Echoles is still putting it all together to become a more consistent pass-rusher, but the traits are present for him to blossom into a complete defensive tackle.

Prospects Considered : DL David Stone, Oklahoma; CB Ellis Robinson IV, Georgia; OL Trevor Lauck, Iowa

14. Minnesota Vikings: RB Jadan Baugh, Florida

Team Fit : Kyler Murray will have an opportunity to prove himself this fall as the Minnesota Vikings' starting quarterback. Depending on his performance, a very different conversation could occur next offseason. As of now, the organization can draft Florida's Jadan Baugh, add the class' top running back and provide the lineup with a new offensive focal point.

Scout's Take : Baugh blends great size (6'1", 225 lbs), vision, patience, burst and physicality. He fits multiple running schemes and is an effective receiver out of the backfield. Despite a bigger frame, the junior prospect will make defenders miss and change directions in addition to finishing runs with power. Baugh should be viewed as a legitimate three-down running back.

Prospects Considered : TE Jamari Johnson, Oregon; Edge Will Heldt, Clemson; IOL Kade Pieper, Iowa

15. Jacksonville Jaguars: DL David Stone, Oklahoma

Team Fit : The Jacksonville Jaguars are set on the edges with Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker. The same can't be said about the defensive interior. Arik Armstead and DaVon Hamilton are both free agents after this season. Oklahoma's David Stone has a high ceiling with enough potential to create an instant impact.

Scout's Take : Stone doesn't have the experience scouts typically like to see, with only two career starts before this season. However, his traits will be difficult to match with his strength, athleticism and near 35-inch arms. Stone is already a good run-defender and shows the movement skills to develop as a pass-rusher.

Prospects Considered : OT Jordan Seaton, LSU; DL A'Mauri Washington, Oregon; WR Nick Marsh, Indiana

16. Chicago Bears: CB Ellis Robinson IV, Georgia

Team Fit : In order for the Chicago Bears to play complementary football, secondary reinforcements will be necessary. This past offseason, the organization reset the safety position with the free-agent signing of Coby Bryant and first-round selection of Dillon Thieneman. Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson is a free agent after this season. Georgia's Ellis Robinson IV presents significant promise as a pure cover corner.

Scout's Take : As the best athlete among the class' top corners, Robinson has immense upside thanks to his recovery ability, ball skills and zone coverage prowess. He's an instinctual route-identifier, who's a little undersized but aggressive in his approach.

Prospects Considered : OT Jordan Seaton, LSU; Edge Will Heldt, Clemson; RB Kewan Lacy, Ole Miss

17. Dallas Cowboys (via Green Bay): TE Jamari Johnson, Oregon

Team Fit : The idea of adding an athlete of Jamari Johnson's caliber to an already potent Dallas Cowboys offense is downright frightening. Jake Ferguson is a steady and reliable target for quarterback Dak Prescott, but he doesn't stress opposing defenses. Johnson can make life easier on all of Dallas' skill position talent.

Scout's Take : Jamari Johnson is an instant mismatch tight end, because he brings the body type and athleticism required to be a three-down threat. His ball skills and route-running nuance should lead to a breakout season for the Oregon Ducks, where he'll have a chance to outshine former teammate Kenyon Sadiq.

Prospects Considered : CB Zabien Brown, Alabama; OT Trevor Lauck, Iowa; LB Chris Cole, Georgia

18. Cincinnati Bengals: OT Jordan Seaton, LSU

Team Fit : Jordan Seaton doesn't necessarily fit the mold the Cincinnati Bengals prefer along their offensive line. Typically, the organization prioritizes mammoth blockers, who are difficult to circumnavigate due to sheer size. However, Seaton's significant upside, coupled with a desire to keep Joe Burrow healthy, makes his selection far too tempting to pass.

Scout's Take : Seaton is the most physically gifted draft-eligible blocker entering the season based primarily on his movement skills in pass protection—which match those of high-end NFL starters. Seaton's twitch and explosiveness are evident but his physical, aggressive demeanor as a finisher warrants legitimate hype entering the season, even if his technique in the run game requires work.

Prospects Considered : CB Zabien Brown, Alabama; RB Ahmad Hardy, Missouri; TE Trey'Dez Green, LSU;

19. Tampa Bay Buccaneers: TE Trey'Dez Green, LSU

Team Fit : Baker Mayfield's contract situation must be settled over the next six months. As of now, he should be expected to re-sign, even though it's not a given. With Mayfield at quarterback, the Buccaneers continue to build around him by adding a mismatch at tight end with a huge catch radius in LSU's Trey'Dez Green. The junior prospect would complement Cade Otton nicely.

Scout's Take : Green is listed at 6'7" and 240 pounds, which opens eyes before he even takes the field. He's still learning the nuances of the position, but he's a problem down the seam of opposing defenses and good at creating yards after the catch.

Prospects Considered : DL A'Mauri Washington, Oregon; OL Trevor Lauck, Iowa; Edge Boubacar Traore, Notre Dame

20. New York Jets (via Dallas): CB Zabien Brown, Alabama

Team Fit : The New York Jets' third and final first-round draft pick provides a potential playmaker in the secondary. The Jets added plenty to the defense this past offseason, but Nahshon Wright is a free agent next year. Furthermore, Brandon Stephens and Jarvis Brownlee Jr. will be entering the final years of their current deals during the 2027 campaign.

Scout's Take : Alabama's Zabien Brown brings a sound run-defender and open-space tackler to the boundary, who stays responsible throughout the play. At this point, he's better in zone coverage than man, but he has the length and athleticism to grow in man and press coverage. An explosive, downhill move gives the 20-year-old a leg up on plays working on the perimeter.

Prospects Considered : OL Trevor Lauck, Iowa; LB Chris Cole, Georgia; S KJ Bolden, Georgia

21. Denver Broncos: WR Nick Marsh, Indiana

Team Fit : In order for the Denver Broncos to reach their full potential, Bo Nix must establish himself as a top-tier starter. Nix showed tremendous growth during his second season, but he can be better. The addition of another weapon to pair with Jaylen Waddle and Troy Franklin will make life easier on the quarterback and more difficult on defenses. In this case, Nick Marsh's physical profile makes him Courtland Sutton's eventual replacement.

Scout's Take : Marsh has a prototypical X-receiver frame and strength after the catch to isolate him on an island. Marsh's build-up speed can stress a defense vertically, while presenting a big target down the sideline on contested catches. The 6'3", 210-pound receiver is also a deceptive route-runner, with head fakes and stop/start traits to lose defenders.

Prospects Considered : Edge Will Heldt, Clemson; CB Jyaire Hill, Michigan; RB Kewan Lacy, Ole Miss

22. San Francisco 49ers: IOL Kade Pieper, Iowa

Team Fit : The center position is often overlooked despite its importance, particularly in the Shanahan system. This season, the San Francisco 49ers will field the league's oldest offensive line, including the elder statesman among NFL centers. Jake Brendel turns 34 later this week, and he isn't signed beyond this season. Iowa's Kade Pieper is transitioning over the ball this fall, but he has all of the tools to excel at center.

Scout's Take : Pieper is another ultra-twitchy prospect, who is similarly light but also has a longer-looking frame than Iowa predecessors Tyler Linderbaum and Logan Jones. Pieper's burst off of the ball and lateral quickness are special enough for the 49ers to consider going against their norm of investing premium draft capital at center for the Shanahan system.

Prospects Considered : Edge Will Heldt, Clemson; S KJ Bolden, Georgia; WR Mario Craver, Texas A&M

23. New England Patriots: Edge Will Heldt, Clemson

Team Fit : On paper, the New England Patriots appear set at the edge of their defense. In reality, the situation is far more fluid. Harold Landry III continues to deal with injuries. Dre'Mont Jones has never registered more than seven sacks in a season. Gabe Jacas enters his rookie campaign with significant expectations, but he needs to prove himself on the field. Another investment in a high-end edge-defender can help solidify New England's defense.

Scout's Take : The selling point for Clemson's Will Heldt is simple: He's a big guy who can move. The 6'6", 260-pound edge-defender can win with power and a long-arm move as a pass-rusher. He also has a nice inside spin move as a counter. Heldt might be a bit of a projection as a first-round pick, but he has the traits to get there with a strong 2026 season.

Prospects Considered : Edge Yhonzae Pierre, Alabama; DL A'Mauri Washington, Oregon; RB Ahmad Hardy, Missouri

24. Houston Texans: RB Ahmad Hardy, Missouri

Team Fit : The Houston Texans traded for David Montgomery this offseason to give the offense a physical lead back. Montgomery will be 30 next year, though. Also, the organization can easily save $7.2 million toward the 2027 salary cap with the veteran's release. Missouri's Ahmad Hardy can immediately serve as an offensive focal point and form a strong one-two punch alongside Woody Marks.

Scout's Take : Hardy is a bowling ball of a runner with elite contact balance, great patience and the vision to find lanes at the line of scrimmage. The consensus All-American excels at attacking the line of scrimmage without overrunning his blocks. He epitomizes a volume runner and gets stronger as the game goes on.

Prospects Considered : OL Trevor Lauck, Iowa; Edge Boubacar Traore, Notre Dame; WR Ryan Coleman-Williams, Alabama

25. Philadelphia Eagles: Edge Yhonzae Pierre, Alabama

Team Fit : The Philadelphia Eagles always seem to be reloading along their defensive front. Yhonzae Pierre's addition may seem like overkill, but Arnold Ebiketie and AJ Epenesa aren't signed beyond this season. Furthermore, both contracts for Nolan Smith and Jalyx Hunt only run through the 2027 campaign. For a team that wants to attack opposing quarterbacks in waves, more depth will be a necessity.

Scout's Take : Pierre can add to his pass-rush arsenal since he relies heavily on turning speed-to-power and a decent long-arm move. Even so, the 6'3", 253-pound prospect flashes impressive movement skills and traits worth betting on. It will also be interesting to see if Alabama expands Pierre's role this fall by giving him more opportunities to defend the run.

Prospects Considered : CB Jyaire Hill, Michigan; S KJ Bolden, Georgia; OL Trevor Lauck, Iowa

26. Kansas City Chiefs: OT Trevor Lauck, Iowa

Team Fit : The Kansas City Chiefs experience a cyclical approach to their offensive line. Either the organization invests too heavily or too little in the position group. The latter is now true, specifically at right tackle, where Jaylon Moore finally takes over as a full-time starter. However, Moore isn't signed beyond this season and may not perform well anyhow. A permanent solution is needed on the strong side.

Scout's Take : Iowa's Trevor Lauck looks like a compact, technically sound collegiate tackle in the mold of another former Hawkeye, Riley Reiff. Lauck could easily move to the right side and provide the Chiefs a well-rounded, reliable blocker, especially as the fourth- or fifth-best starter among their offensive line hierarchy.

Prospects Considered : OT Carter Smith, Indiana; WR Charlie Becker, Indiana; S KJ Bolden, Georgia

27. Detroit Lions: CB Kelley Jones, Mississippi State

Team Fit : The Detroit Lions' top three cornerbacks are either not signed beyond this season (Rock Ya-Sin and Roger McCreary) or have no guaranteed money left on their deal in 2027 (D.J. Reed). Another first-round investment in the secondary could give the Lions what they expected when the organization drafted Terrion Arnold in the first round of the 2024 class.

Scout's Take : As a former safety, Mississippi State's Kelley Jones shows strong route recognition and spacing in zone coverage. He has the body type (6'3", 200 lbs) to play on the boundary in man coverage but needs to clean up his footwork and hand-usage. When those traits are combined with his ball skills and tracking ability, Jones has the ability to take a big next step this season.

Prospects Considered : CB Jyaire Hill, Michigan; S KJ Bolden, Georgia; Edge Boubacar Traore, Notre Dame

28. Los Angeles Chargers: Edge Boubacar Traore, Notre Dame

Team Fit : The selection of Akheem Mesidor in this year's first round isn't enough, not when Khalil Mack and Bud Dupree are set to be free agents after this season. The Los Angeles Chargers should bolster their pass rush during next year's draft, with Notre Dame's Boubacar Traore joining Mesidor and Tuli Tuipulotu as an exciting trio.

Scout's Take : Notre Dame didn't trust Traore to play the run last year, using him primarily in passing situations and sitting him entirely against Navy's triple-option offense. The 21-year-old prospect will need to show growth in that department this fall and become a more complete player for the next level. Regardless, Traore makes his money as a pass rusher, where his lateral movement skills and a nasty spin move really shine.

Prospects Considered : OL Carter Smith, Indiana; CB Jyaire Hill, Michigan; DL A'Mauri Washington

29. Baltimore Ravens: RB Kewan Lacy, Ole Miss

Team Fit : Eventually, Derrick Henry is going to wear down and no longer dominate. That time may still be a few years from now, but the Baltimore Ravens can take some pressure off the 32-year-old ball-carrier to maximize his final years, while setting up a seamless transition at running back. Ole Miss' Kewan Lacy lacks Henry's size. However, the prospect definitely brings big-play ability.

Scout's Take : Lacy is a talented runner with short-area quickness to make defenders miss in the open field. He's also a long-strider, who slashes and cuts through opposing defenses. The 20-year-old prospect is a three-down running back with plus-marks in pass protection and receiving ability.

Prospects Considered : DL Ahmad Moten Sr., Miami; IOL Greg Johnson, Minnesota; CB OJ Frederique Jr., Miami

30. Seattle Seahawks: Edge Matayo Uiagalelei, Oregon

Team Fit : The Seattle Seahawks are old on the edges of their defense. DeMarcus Lawrence is 34 and entering his final professional season. Uchenna Nwosu, who turns 30 later this year, is a free agent after this season. Dante Fowler Jr., 32, is only signed through this season. Oregon's Matayo Uiagalelei showed he can come up with big plays when necessary to open this year's college football season, which makes him the perfect addition in Seattle's aggressive defense.

Scout's Take : Uiagalelei offers some scheme/alignment versatility with his experience playing as a stand-up outside linebacker, while having the size to be a base end. The 6'5", 265-pound edge-defender is a solid all-around player, who can set the edge against the run and be a productive pass-rusher with 18.5 sacks during his first three years at Oregon.

Prospects Considered : OL Carter Smith, Indiana; DL A'Mauri Washington, Oregon; WR Charlie Becker, Indiana

31. Buffalo Bills: DT A'Mauri Washington, Oregon

Team Fit : The Buffalo Bills' Deone Walker may be built like a traditional nose tackle, but his game says otherwise. Something similar can be said about Oregon's A'Mauri Washington, though he's more powerful at the point of attack because he plays with better leverage. Washington is more disruptive than a traditional space-eater. Even so, he can be an invaluable addition along Buffalo's new-look defensive front.

Scout's Take : Washington is still putting it all together as a pass-rusher, but his size (6'3", 325 lbs), strength and athleticism give him a high ceiling at the next level. The Oregon product is already a good run defender with the potential to develop into a three-down defensive tackle thanks to impressive physical traits.

Prospects Considered : WR Charlie Becker, Indiana; OL Cayden Green, Missouri; DL Anthony Smith, Minnesota

32. Cleveland Browns (via LA Rams): DL Ahmad Moten Sr., Miami

Team Fit : Once the Cleveland Browns have their new quarterback in place, general manager Andrew Berry can continue to build upon an already strong core of young talent. While the Browns already have Mason Graham in place, Cleveland can replace veteran Maliek Collins, who turns 32 next year. Miami's Ahmad Moten Sr. brings a similar skill set to Collins, which should allow the new interior defender to fit in nicely.

Scout's Take : Moten arguably has the best first step among the entire 2027 defensive tackle class. He's a gap-shooter, who can get penetration, and offers value as an interior pass-rusher. However, the Hurricane might get tabbed as a scheme-specific player since he can have issues holding his gap when taking on blocks.

Prospects Considered : IOL Greg Johnson, Minnesota; Edge Kenyatta Jackson, Ohio State; CB Brice Pollock, Texas Tech

articles.title: Ranking the 10 Best Last-Place Fantasy Football Punishments
articles.summary: All summer long, fantasy football managers do their best to draft a team that will lead them to a championship. Then come months of trying to win matchups, playing the waiver wire, making trades and hoping to hit the stretch run in good shape.
articles.body:
All summer long, fantasy football managers do their best to draft a team that will lead them to a championship. Then come months of trying to win matchups, playing the waiver wire, making trades and hoping to hit the stretch run in good shape.

Fall gives way to winter. The fantasy playoffs arrive. And then right around Christmas, one fortunate soul is crowned the champion. Glory follows. Fame. Perhaps a trophy of some sort.

But for every champion who finishes first, there's a team that must finish last. And in many fantasy football leagues, that last-place manager doesn't just suffer the indignity of the standings. They must be punished.

As fantasy football has exploded in popularity, so have last-place punishments. They have become increasingly varied and elaborate. Some are a little mean. Many more are abjectly hilarious. All are embarrassing to one degree or another.

If you're looking for a relatively tame and inexpensive punishment that still makes the last-place manager in your league feel like a doofus, then this might be the one for you.

There are several directions you can go here. With the explosion in fantasy football's popularity, numerous sites sell last-place trophies in all shapes and sizes. You can find all sorts of "I Suck at Fantasy Football" T-shirts, chains and other doodads. All send the same message.

"I had a rotten fantasy season. And the jerks I play with aren't about to let me forget it."

We do this in the King's Classic Dick Butkus Division draft that occurs every year at the Pro Football Hall of Fame. In fact, every team that doesn't win the championship gets something to remind them that they didn't win the championship.

If you want to take this one up a notch, stipulate that the trophy must me prominently displayed in the last-place manager's home, so he can spend a year answering questions about it from everyone who comes over.

By now, most of you have probably seen or at least heard of the Hot Ones podcast, where celebrities and athletes answer interview questions while eating chicken wings that vary in intensity from "that wasn't too bad" to "Da Bomb Beyond Insanity."

Well, this punishment borrows the premise for that podcast—and murders every taste bud your last-place manager has.

Just like the show, the last-place manager will take part in an "interview." But instead of softball questions about their favorite co-stars or acting techniques, they get to answer questions about their most embarrassing moments, fears or whatever else you can think of—all while eating wings that ramp up from "OK, that's a little hot" to "I think my face is melting."

Keep the questions from getting so personal that they land someone in divorce court. While these punishments may seem harsh, they are based on good-natured fun.

But outside of that, the only boundaries here are your own creativity—and the gastrointestinal fortitude of the poor last-place finisher who has to eat those wings.

Oh, and it must all be recorded for posterity , of course.

This is one of the better-known last-place punishments.

The rules are easy enough: The last-place manager has to go to Waffle House (or any other restaurant that's open all 24 hours) and stay there for a full day. However, they can eat their way home. Every waffle, order of hash browns and sausage link deducts a predetermined amount of time from their sentence.

As always, proper attire (The "I suck at fantasy football" shirt) is a must. Recording the event for posterity is recommended. Leaguemates showing up to heckle is encouraged.

This punishment isn't ranked higher because, frankly, it's not that bad. So long as the restaurant has Wi-Fi, I can show up early, get my grub on, and with any luck, be out by evening. Might have a bit of a tummyache, but them's the breaks.

But if you want to make this a true challenge, flip the restaurant from Waffle House to White Castle. Fourteen hours of pounding belly bombs and onion nuggets are bound to take their toll at some point.

There are a million variations to this theme, but they all share a few things in common.

The first is one of those "I suck at fantasy football" T-shirts we mentioned.

The second is making the last-place manager go somewhere very public wearing said shirt, and do something they'd really rather not.

As in the tweet above, you can have them attend a game or practice wearing a rival's gear, which will quickly make them all sorts of new friends.

You can make them go to the grocery store wearing a garish outfit and stop every person they meet to tell them, "I suck at fantasy football."

Make the last-place manager perform at a comedy club's "Open Mic Night." Or perform a song chosen by the rest of the league at karaoke.

One particularly popular variation is "date night." The last-place manager has to not only go to a restaurant wearing said garish outfit and making said proclamations, but they also must take a stuffed animal or blow-up doll along as a "date"—and talk to it.

Helpful hint—call ahead to the restaurant and give them a heads-up. No one needs the cops getting called.

Whatever the variation, the point is the same: public embarrassment. The more public, the better.

OK, now things are starting to get mean—in a good way.

This is another punishment with any number of variations. But at its core, they are all the same. It's a combination of public humiliation and fundraising, whether it's for charity or to help pay for draft-day festivities.

Do it for charity. It's good for the soul.

The most popular variation of this punishment is the lemonade stand. The last-place manager must open a lemonade stand just like when they were a kid. Then they either have to raise a predetermined amount of money or stay out there for a predetermined amount of time.

Now, some have taken the theme and ramped it up a notch or six. If there's an area near you where street performers gather, you can dress the last-place manager up in a ridiculous outfit and make them get their music on.

Flying to Vegas and dressing up like Elvis is admittedly taking this to extremes. But to be fair, the guy did finish last two years in a row.

For this writer, this might be the most abjectly terrifying punishment on this list. I would rather dress up like Pikachu and sing country music for six hours at a mall than ever take another test again.

But finish in last place in a league with this punishment, and it's back to school for you.

The premise is simple: The last-place manager has to take the SAT or ACT. Either works.

The humiliation here is threefold. First, you have to take several hours out of your day to re-take a test you haven't thought about (much less studied for) for years. You have to take that test in a room full of teenagers while wearing the ever-present "I suck at fantasy football" shirt, which is going to get you gawked at the entire time.

Lastly, once you get the results of your triumphant return to academia, you have to post them on social media for all to see—and ridicule.

For most of us dummies, those results aren't getting you into Yale.

What says friendship and camaraderie more than making someone parade around a neighborhood full of strangers making a complete fool of themselves?

One variation on the scavenger hunt theme that got a lot of traction on social media was a league where the last-place finisher had to go trick-or-treating. Except it was nowhere near Halloween, and he's a grown man.

Until he got 10 pieces of candy, he was knocking on doors and getting glared at.

It doesn't have to be candy, though. You can dress the last-place manager up any way you wish and send them on a quest for whatever. A very particular list of canned goods. A list of random items that are neither especially easy to track down nor too obscure.

The key here is taking the last-place manager to unfamiliar surroundings. Let them knock on doors near their own home, and their pesky neighbors could be motivated to help them.

This might be the most insidious punishment on this list. Or at least it would be with my friends—bunch of savages, I tell ya.

This punishment works best if the draft is held at someone's house, not the local watering hole. But if it's the latter, it can still be done. The last-place manager just has to pick up the tab—either in its entirety, just for the champion or up to a set amount. Whatever works.

However, since that is just expensive and not humiliating, every time someone orders something, the last-place manager must say something like, "Sure, Carl, I will gladly buy you an onion blossom because you are so much better at fantasy football than me"—loudly.

If the draft is at a private residence, it's so much worse. The last-place manager has to play gopher on draft day for the entire league.

If Carl wants a ginger ale, you have to get up and give him one. Someone wants Doritos? You have to get up again and get them. The draft becomes hours of your "friends" making you play fetch. Over and over and over.

If that's not diabolical enough, the last-place manager can be forced to prepare the draft-day food. Pay for it. Serve it dressed as a French maid.

As with most of these punishments, the variations on the theme are endless.

I would give a month's salary for the video of this punishment. But the guy I heard it from insisted that he and his leaguemates don't record it. It's just between the 12 of them...and all of the other people who see it, of course.

The last-place manager dresses in the omnipresent "I Suck" shirt, shorts and flip-flops. Nothing else. They also wear a sign so garish it can be seen from space.

The rest of the league dons long black robes—think Grim Reaper Halloween costumes with the hood and all that good stuff. They all have large bells.

Then, the whole group goes outside the last-place manager's home and walks up and down the street re-enacting the "Walk of Shame" from Game of Thrones —but with less nudity and vegetable throwing. Again, no one wants the cops called.

This punishment amuses me to no end. It has costumes. Props. And the humiliation is turned up to 11. This poor schlub isn't just being embarrassed in front of strangers. These are the last-place manager's neighbors. People he or she sees regularly.

And now those neighbors know the manager's darkest secret: He or she sucks at fantasy football.

First off, don't just copy this last-place punishment. To do so is to do this masterpiece of idiocy a disservice. It's completely ridiculous. It's obviously quite embarrassing. My guy is leaning into it with everything he has. And it is unique.

OK, there's a new one I'm most terrified by. NO ONE needs to see this writer with a speedo on.

We all have no shortage of seriousness in our lives. Fantasy football is supposed to be an escape from that. And while humiliation is most assuredly a part of any good last-place punishment, it's not mean-spirited. It's friends having fun at one another's expense, which is as old as friendship itself.

Last-place punishments are an extension of the personalities of the managers in a league. And in most leagues that have them, those managers know each other well. Make the last-place punishment yours as a group. And if that last-place punishment becomes yours in the way no one wants it to be, be like the Very Hungry Caterpillar and give it your all. Get the family involved.

You never know. You might go viral. Wind up on the Today show . Achieve fantasy football immortality.

Even if you have to finish last to do it.

articles.title: 49ers' Christian McCaffrey Hypes Australia Game After Admitting There Were 'A Lot of Question Marks'
articles.summary: While presenting a massive departure from the team's usual pregame preparations, San Francisco 49ers star Christian McCaffrey said the trip to Australia has been a "cool experience."
articles.body:
While presenting a massive departure from the team's usual pregame preparations, San Francisco 49ers star Christian McCaffrey said the trip to Australia has been a "cool experience."

"There's a lot of question marks when you hear you're playing in Australia, but since we've been here, it's been so cool," he told reporters over the weekend. "The people are unbelievable. The food's incredible. The coffee's great. The atmosphere, you can already feel it. And it's been a lot of fun, so we're super fired up we're here."

Melbourne, Australia, is 17 hours ahead of the West Coast of the United States. The Niners will be kicking off against the Los Angeles Rams at 10:35 a.m. local time Friday in order to make a Thursday prime-time slot in the United States.

You could almost witness the brain of Niners coach Kyle Shanahan overloading when he tried to work through the conversion:

The time difference had an important component for Shanahan. Rather than having to submit his injury report on Monday in Melbourne, he could wait until Tuesday because that would be Monday in the United States.

"We're technically in the future from where we're from, and the Rams are in the present," he told reporters . "I don't have to talk about injuries until tomorrow. So, I'm not talking about them."

Whereas the Niners arrived in Australia last week, the Rams veered in the opposite direction. Los Angeles is heading out Tuesday with the idea keeping the game-week schedule as normal as possible.

That seems a little counterintuitive because it leaves less time to overcome the inevitable jet lag on a flight from the United States to Australia. The Rams also won't be able to fully enjoy a setting they may otherwise never experience.

It sounds as though McCaffrey had some reservations about playing so far from home but has come to savor the locale.
